ODDLY MADRAS · SS'26

Confidence
without noise.

A guide to representing ODDLY.

01 — Brand Architecture

One brand.
Many collections.

ODDLY is built in two layers. A master brand that never changes, and a series of seasonal collections that each dress it in a new world. Understanding this is the key to representing ODDLY.

The master brand
The constant underneath everything

The master brand is monochrome, quiet, and permanent.

The ODDLY identity — its logo, its black-and-white world, its voice, the way it holds itself — stays the same no matter the season. It is the thread a returning customer recognises. When you represent the brand at the master level (the profile, the brand film, the about page), it speaks in black and white and lets the clothing hold the colour.

The seasonal collection

Each collection is its own world, built the same way.

A collection brings its own name, palette, elements and mood.

1 · Master artwork
One composed illustration per collection. The source everything else is drawn from.
2 · Derived compositions
Panels cropped from the master for posts, title cards and collaterals.
3 · Photography world
A backdrop, a light, a set of props — the season’s environment.
4 · The feed
Where it all meets the audience, in a planned grid.

A sneak peek at the structure — each layer is covered in detail further down this guide.

The same structure, two different worlds.

How to use this

Represent the season through its arc.

When you plan a campaign or a month of content, move through the collection’s chapters rather than posting at random. The arc gives the feed a shape and the customer a journey. The next collection will have its own name and its own chapters — the two-layer structure stays exactly the same.

02 — Logo

The mark.

The ODDLY / MADRAS lockup is the single most protected element of the brand. Use it exactly as supplied. When in doubt, give it room and leave it alone.

Never redrawn
The two marks

ODDLY has two approved marks. The full lockup — the ring above the wordmark — and the wordmark alone. Both exist in black and white. Use the full lockup wherever there is room to let it breathe; use the wordmark when space is tight or the ring would read too small.

The full lockup

Ring above the wordmark, MADRAS spaced beneath. The primary mark.

The wordmark

ODDLY with MADRAS beneath, no ring. For small sizes and tight spaces.

Always use “Oddly Madras” as the full name. Either mark may be centre-aligned or left-aligned to suit the layout, but the internal proportions never change.

Clear spaceKeep a margin of at least the height of the “O” on all sides. Nothing intrudes.
Minimum sizeFull lockup: never below 90px wide on screen. Below that, switch to the wordmark.
ColourBlack or white only. The logo never takes on a collection colour.
PlacementGive it a calm, uncluttered field. Corners or centre, with breathing room.
Getting it right

Protect the mark.

Do
  • Use the supplied files as-is
  • Black or white, full clear space
  • Calm, uncluttered background
  • Original proportions preserved
Don’t
  • Don’t stretch, rotate or recolour
  • Don’t place on a busy image
  • Don’t crowd it or shrink it away
  • Don’t recreate it in another font
03 — Colour

Colour is a state
of feeling.

Not a statement. The ODDLY identity is monochrome; the collections breathe colour in, one season at a time, always through the same law. When you represent the brand, you work in black and white — and you borrow the season’s palette only for the season’s content.

The identity
The master palette

Black and white. Always.

Profile, logo, brand-level typography, packaging, the master voice on a page — all monochrome. This is what keeps ODDLY recognisable while every drop reinvents its palette around it.

Black · #000000
White · #FFFFFF
The governing law
The colour philosophy

How every ODDLY colour must feel.

Whatever the season, colour obeys the same character. This is the law you apply to any future collection’s content — it does not change when the palette does.

Botanical
Soft
Grounded
Modern
Expressive
Warm
01Saturation. No pure or raw hues. Medium-to-low chroma only — every bright filtered through grey, milkiness or warmth.
02Depth. Darks are allowed, but greyed and quiet — never sharp contrast.
03Anchors & accents. Four anchor families every season (soft off-white · botanical green · soft floral · one calm cool). One or two accents, never dominant. Darks paired with lighter shades.
Changes every drop
The philosophy, applied

One colourway represents the season.

A collection carries many colourways in the clothing — but for digital assets we choose a single one that best represents the drop. That colour becomes the season’s accent, and a small analogous range extends from it. Everything else stays black and white.

This is how a collection announces itself online without ever disturbing the master identity.

Choose oneA single colourway per collection becomes the digital accent.
Extend analogouslyNeighbouring tones only — a tint, a shade, an adjacent hue.
Keep it an accentThe accent supports; black and white still carry the brand.
It must obey the lawMuted, filtered, calm. Never a raw hue.
04 — Typography

Two voices,
one quiet register.

Besley carries every heading; Fredoka carries every word of body. The emphasis lives in the serif — the body never raises its voice. Together they read warm, editorial, and calm.

The type system
Headings
Besley
Warm slab serif · titles, headlines, the wordmark
The Secret Garden
Samaya · Kimaya · Ela
worth looking at twice

Regular · Medium · SemiBold · Bold — SemiBold for most headings and product names.

Body
Fredoka
Soft humanist sans · body, captions, labels

It feels simple at first, but the closer you look, the more there is to discover. Body copy stays light and generously spaced — quiet on the page, never bold.

Light (300) & Regular (400) only. Never the bold weights.

Headings → BesleyProduct names, titles, section heads, pull quotes.
Body → FredokaCaptions, labels, paragraphs, colourway names.
Weight contrastLives in Besley. Fredoka stays uniformly light.
NeverBold Fredoka. Substituting either typeface. Tight body leading.
05 — Voice & Tone

Write the way
she notices.

ODDLY speaks quietly, in the second person and the present tense. Every line wraps a plain product fact inside a feeling. It observes; it never sells. That character is constant — but it is spoken in two registers, depending on whether the reader is a buyer or a customer.

The constant voice
The voice, in four qualities
Second person, present tense“You keep finding small things to appreciate.” Spoken to her, now.
Feeling around factThe product detail is stated plainly, then wrapped in a quiet observation.
Room to breatheShort lines, generous breaks. Never a dense block of copy.
Calm, never loudNo “Shop now”, no urgency, no exclamation marks, no emoji.
Two registers
Audience decides the register

One voice. Two registers.

The four qualities above never change — ODDLY is always calm, observant and unhurried. What changes is register: how much specialist language we use, and how much we explain. ODDLY produces print and digital media for two quite different audiences, and each needs a different level of fluency.

Get the register wrong and the work fails in one of two ways: a buyer finds us naïve, or a customer finds us aloof. Choosing correctly is the single most consequential decision in an ODDLY caption or lookbook.

Register one
The Atelier

Speaks to people who already know fashion. Its job is to demonstrate command of the craft — to place ODDLY credibly among designers, not merchants.

Audience — boutiques and stockists, buyers, press, industry, collaborators.
Used in — trade lookbooks, line sheets, press releases, wholesale decks, brand films.
Vocabulary — precise garment and technique terms used without apology: pin-tuck, appliqué, bias, dropped shoulder, hand-run seam, GSM, handwoven.
Structure — longer, composed sentences. Construction described before effect. Nothing explained twice.
Proves — expertise, intention, restraint.
Register two
The Counter

Speaks to the woman buying the garment. Its job is to make the craft legible and welcoming — knowledgeable without ever being a lecture.

Audience — customers in store, at pop-ups, and online.
Used in — pop-up and event material, retail lookbooks, product pages, social captions, WhatsApp and DMs.
Vocabulary — the same technique named, then translated: “pin-tucks — tiny hand-stitched folds”. Mildly technical, never opaque.
Structure — short sentences. Effect described before construction. Says what it means for her.
Proves — care, ease, honesty.

Both registers are ODDLY. Neither is a simplified version of the other — one demonstrates fluency, the other extends it.

The same garment, both registers

Same truth, told to a different room.

A worked example on Samaya, the pin-tuck shirt. Notice the facts do not change — only the fluency assumed of the reader.

The Atelier

Samaya. Rows of closely set pin-tucks compress the sleeve head, giving the shirt its structure without adding volume. Cut in handwoven linen and finished with hand-worked appliqué. Made to order.

Technique first. No translation offered — none needed.

The Counter

This is Samaya. Those fine folds along the sleeve are pin-tucks, stitched by hand — they hold the shape so the shirt keeps its shoulder all day. It’s linen, so it breathes, and it softens each time you wear it.

Effect first. The term is named, then explained in the same breath.

The caption template

Every post, the same quiet shape.

This is the structure behind an ODDLY caption. Follow the shape; change the words.

Some things are worth looking at twice.

Kimaya pairs rows of pin-tucks with floral appliqué that slowly reveals itself the closer you look.

It feels simple at first, but the closer you look, the more there is to discover.

Part of The Secret Garden.

#oddlymadras #slowfashion #thesecretgarden
1 · Hook — one quiet, near-aphoristic line that sets a feeling.
2 · Product — name the garment and its detail, plainly.
3 · The turn — a reflective beat that echoes the hook.
4 · Anchor — “Part of [Collection].”
5 · Tags — three only: brand · category · collection.
Getting it right

Say it like ODDLY, not like a sale.

Do
“You wear it the way you inhabit a good day — without thinking about it at all. Bhumi, in Moon Wash. Part of The Secret Garden.”
  • Quiet, second-person, present tense
  • Feeling wrapped around the piece
  • Three considered hashtags
Don’t
“NEW DROP 🌸✨ Shop the Bhumi co-ord NOW before it sells out!! Link in bio 🛍️ #ootd #fashion #musthave #sale”
  • Urgency, hype, exclamation, emoji
  • Sells the transaction, not the feeling
  • Scattershot trend hashtags
06 — Instagram

A showroom,
not a shop.

Instagram is ODDLY’s primary channel — but it is not a sales channel. Its purpose is to establish how the brand is perceived. A post has done its work when it has strengthened the brand’s standing — not when it has moved a unit, or collected a certain number of likes.

What the channel is for

Two purposes. Nothing else.

Purpose one
Presence & identity

Instagram is the brand’s public face. It is where ODDLY’s aesthetic is established, where recognition is built, and where reputation is held.

It is also the front door for collaborations and enquiries — for most collaborators, press and stockists, the account is their first encounter with the brand and the channel through which they make contact.

Purpose two
Anticipation

Keeping the audience aware of what is coming — collections, drops, pop-ups and events.

The work is to build quiet expectation, so that when something arrives the community is already waiting for it rather than discovering it.

What it is not for

We are not selling here.

ODDLY does not use Instagram to close transactions, and does not measure a post by what it converts. Equally, the account does not compete for attention: we do not chase virality, likes or shares. Reach that arrives by diluting the brand costs more than it returns.

This is a liberating position, and it should be used as one. Freed from performance metrics, every post can be judged on a single question: does this make ODDLY look like the house we intend it to be?

The standard
Production values

Low-effort content is never published.

Premium is not a filter applied at the end — it is decided at the point of making. If something was quick and easy to produce, it does not belong on the account.

Photography & videoCampaign standard only. Considered light, composition and grade — never a phone snap pressed into service.
MusicCurated and chosen to suit the piece. Never trending audio.
EffortIf it took no effort to make, it will look like it. Post less rather than post lightly.
FormatsThe same standard governs feed, Reels and Stories. There is no “off-duty” surface.
Getting it right

The difference between premium and passable.

Do
  • Publish only campaign-standard imagery and film
  • Choose music deliberately, for the piece
  • Let a considered post sit longer; post less often
  • Judge work by how it makes the brand read
Don’t
  • Reach for a trending audio to borrow attention
  • Fill a gap with something quick
  • Post to keep a schedule alive
  • Chase a format because it performs elsewhere
Sound

Every collection has a sound.

A collection is a mood, and a mood has a sound as surely as it has a palette. Audio is not a decoration added when a Reel is edited — it is part of the collection’s identity, and it is decided at the start, alongside the colours and the visual direction. When the collection is conceived, its sound is conceived with it: a defined audio mood — genre, tempo, instrumentation, and a handful of reference tracks — that everything then draws from.

That mood is what carries onto Instagram. Every Reel, every Story with sound, every marketing asset reaches into the same small, related audio palette. The point is not one identical track on repeat, but one recognisable world — so the sound of a post is unmistakably the sound of that collection.

Decided earlyThe audio mood is set at collection kickoff, beside the palette and visual direction — never chosen post by post at the edit.
A small palette, not one trackTwo or three related textures the collection can draw from, tight enough to stay recognisable.
Carried everywhereThe same world runs through Instagram and every marketing asset, so the sound reads as the collection’s own.
Still never trending audioReference tracks and mood guide the choice — not whatever sound is circulating that week.
Do
  • Define the audio mood when the collection is conceived
  • Write it down: genre, tempo, instrumentation, reference tracks
  • Draw every post and asset from that one palette
  • Keep it tight enough to stay recognisable across the season
Don’t
  • Pick audio at the edit, post by post, with no through-line
  • Let one collection wander across unrelated moods and genres
  • Reach for trending audio to fill the gap
  • Treat sound as an afterthought to the visuals
Learn from our own shelves

Secret Garden knew its sound. Dahlia didn’t.

Secret Garden landed on slow piano and held it — the audio was as coherent as the palette, and the collection sounded like itself wherever you met it. Dahlia was the opposite: the audio wandered, with no through-line to tie the posts together, so the collection never built a sound of its own. The difference wasn’t effort at the edit — it was that one mood was decided at the start and the other was left to chance. Decide it early, and every post inherits it.

Judged case by case
Collaborations

Collaborate freely. Protect the grid.

ODDLY collaborates openly. Where a partnership genuinely serves the growth of the business — a designer, a photographer, a stockist, a publication, a person of standing in the field — it is worth doing. There is no fixed list and no standing approval: each opportunity is weighed on its own merits.

The collaboration itself is rarely the question. The question is what it leaves behind on the profile.

The partnership is open

Say yes to work that builds the brand’s standing and reach among the right people. Decided case by case, on the value of the specific opportunity.

The grid is not

If the resulting post does not sit within the grid’s aesthetic, it comes off the grid. The collaboration still happened — the artefact simply does not stay on the profile.

Assess the output firstBefore agreeing, know what will be published and whether it can live on the grid.
Hold the standardA collaboration is not an exemption from production values. The same bar applies.
Remove without frictionTaking a post off the grid is routine housekeeping, not a rejection of the partner.
The grid outranks the postNo single collaboration is worth the coherence of the profile.
How the account is planned
Campaigns

We post in narratives, not in posts.

Nothing goes up in isolation. The account is planned as a sequence of campaigns — cohesive narratives that carry the audience somewhere, rather than a stream of unrelated images.

There is no fixed template. One campaign might open by introducing the collection, move through its sub-collections in turn, and be punctuated along the way with founder pieces to camera — so the account reads as a house with a point of view, and never as a catalogue. The next might take an entirely different shape.

What matters is that a shape is chosen deliberately before anything is posted.

One example of a campaign shape
Introduce
Open the collection — its name, its world, its mood.
Move through
Take the audience across the sub-collections, one passage at a time.
Punctuate
Break the rhythm with founder-to-camera pieces, so it never reads as a catalogue.

Illustrative only — a campaign may run to more or fewer beats, in any order that serves the story.

The rule of three

Everything is planned in multiples of three.

The grid is three tiles wide, so every campaign beat is planned in threes — or sixes, or nines. Rows complete. Nothing is left half-finished at the top of the profile, and no post arrives as an orphan.

This is the discipline that makes the grid read as it does: aesthetic, cohesive and professional, rather than assembled post by post.

Judged case by case
Social proof

Proof, only if it holds the grid.

Press, features, stockist mentions, a customer in the clothes — proof that the brand is loved is worth showing, but not at the cost of how the account reads. The account does not become a wall of screenshots and reposts. Social proof earns a place only when it clears the same bar as everything else: it has to be aesthetic, and it has to sit inside the world of the grid rather than interrupt it.

Because the grid is planned in rows, proof is handled the same way — grouped in threes. A single stray screenshot breaks the line; three considered tiles, composed together, read as a deliberate row and keep the grid whole. If a piece of proof can’t be made to look the part, or can’t be grouped cleanly, it lives in Stories or Highlights instead — not the feed.

Do
  • Show proof only when it’s genuinely aesthetic
  • Plan it in threes, composed as one clean row
  • Re-style or re-shoot proof so it sits in the grid’s world
  • Send anything that doesn’t fit to Stories or Highlights
Don’t
  • Post a lone screenshot that breaks the row
  • Build a wall of reposts and tagged photos
  • Let a low-quality image through because the mention is flattering
  • Chase proof for its own sake, off-palette
How to use this

Three, or not at all.

A single glowing feature or one customer photo, dropped in alone, snaps the grid out of its rhythm. Hold proof back until there are three pieces that can be composed as a row — a feature, a customer in the clothes, a stockist moment — all treated to the same light, crop and palette as the rest of the feed. Grouped and styled, proof becomes another considered row. Ungrouped, it waits, or it lives in Highlights.

Calls to action

Invite, don’t sell.

The rule holds: we do not post to move units, and a caption never reads like a checkout button. “Buy now”, “shop the link”, “limited stock” — none of these belong on the account. But inviting is not selling. When something is live, the community should know, and should feel gently pointed toward it — never pushed.

There are two moments where a call to action is appropriate, and each has its own quiet form.

Collection drops
A new collection is live

Let them know it has arrived.

When a collection goes live, the announcement post may say so — softly, and inside the brand’s voice. The aim is to close the loop for a community that has been watching the collection build: to signal that it is now here, and that the site is where it lives. A single, unhurried line does this. It notes that the collection is live and points to the site; it does not count down, discount, or urge.

Do
  • Note quietly that the collection is now live
  • Point to the site as the place it lives (“now at the link in bio”)
  • Keep it to one unhurried line, in the brand’s voice
  • Let the imagery carry the announcement; the words only confirm it
Don’t
  • Write “buy now”, “shop now” or “order today”
  • Manufacture urgency — countdowns, “limited stock”, “selling fast”
  • Mention price or discount in the caption
  • Repeat the same push across every tile of the drop
How to use this

The link lives in the bio; the caption only nods to it.

Keep the site link in the profile bio, not spelled out in the caption. The post’s job is to say, in the brand’s register, that the collection has arrived — a line like “[Collection] is now with us. Find it at the link in our bio.” The reader who wants more knows exactly where to go, and the post stays an invitation rather than a sale.

Events
Bloom Room & other gatherings

Announce the room. Point to the bio.

For an upcoming Bloom Room, pop-up or event, the announcement post carries the invitation — what it is, when, and the feeling of it — written warmly and in full. Anything transactional (the RSVP link, the form, the guest list sign-up) lives in the profile bio, never in the caption. The post makes people want to be in the room; the bio is where they act on it.

Do
  • Let the caption carry the invitation — the what, when and why
  • Keep the RSVP or sign-up link in the bio
  • Direct people there simply (“RSVP at the link in our bio”)
  • Write it as a welcome, not a ticket sale
Don’t
  • Paste raw links or forms into the caption
  • Frame attendance as a purchase or a scramble for spots
  • Lead with logistics before the feeling of the evening
  • Chase sign-ups with pressure or repeated reminders
07 — Website

Browsed before.
Bought after.

The site is a Shopify build doing two jobs: a virtual catalogue and a point of sale. It is not an e-commerce platform, and it should not be designed like one.

What the site is for

The decision is made in person.

ODDLY garments are rarely bought on impulse. At this price and this level of craft, a customer wants to see the piece in person — to handle the linen, look closely at the embroidery, understand the work in it.

So the site sits on either side of that moment. It is where a customer discovers the pieces before seeing them in person — at a pop-up, or at one of the partner boutiques that stock ODDLY — and where they complete the purchase afterwards if they have gone home to think.

Before
The catalogue. She studies the pieces online and decides what she wants to see.
In person
A pop-up, an event, or a stockist. She touches the cloth, sees the craft, and decides.
After
The counter. She buys there, or returns home and completes it on the site.
What this asks of the design

Show the work. Stay out of the way.

Catalogue firstPhotography and detail carry the site. Show construction, embroidery and cloth clearly enough to be worth travelling for.
No urgency devicesNo countdowns, scarcity banners or hard-sell prompts. They belong to a kind of retail ODDLY is not.
Make returning easySomeone coming back a week after seeing a piece in person should find it and complete the purchase without friction.
Point to where it can be seenPop-ups, events and stockists should all be easy to find. Part of the site’s job is bringing people to the cloth.
08 — Lookbook

One collection.
Several editions.

The lookbook is the collection in printed form — a catalogue of the season. There is no single lookbook: each edition is cut for the room it will be opened in, and the order of its contents is a decision, never a default.

The editions

Three editions, three rooms.

Each edition carries the same collection, but differs in length, register and sequence. Register follows the reader — see Voice & Tone for the distinction between the Atelier and the Counter.

The pop-up edition
For — the customer, in hand at an event.
Register — the Counter.
Length — long. Around thirty pages.
Detail — maximum. Every colourway, every detail shot.
Role — a selling tool. It sits in the room and supports the sales rep in conversation.
The trade edition
For — boutiques, stockists and buyers.
Register — the Atelier. Full designer vocabulary.
Length — edited. Only what earns its place.
Detail — construction and craft foremost.
Role — to establish ODDLY’s standing as a house within the first few pages.
The drop edition
For — a mini or festive drop.
Register — follows the audience it is made for.
Length — short. A handful of pages.
Detail — enough to carry the drop, no more.
Role — to give a small release its own moment without the weight of a full season.
Set per edition
Sequence

The order is the argument.

Two editions can hold identical pieces and do entirely different work, depending on what the reader meets first. Decide the sequence around what that particular reader needs to feel, and in what order.

Trade — lead with the strongest

A buyer forms a judgement in the first few pages. Front-load the most accomplished pieces so the standard of the house is established the moment the book is opened.

Impress first. Explain after.

Pop-up — build toward the occasion

Open with mood, then move through one sub-collection at a time. Begin with the quieter pieces that slip easily into any wardrobe, and build toward the heavily embroidered and appliquéd occasion pieces.

Everyday first. Occasion last.

Decide the sequence deliberatelyNever inherit the last edition’s order by default.
One register per editionSet it at the front and hold it throughout.
Length follows purposeA drop does not need a season’s pagination.
Every edition is the brandA four-page drop book is held to the same standard as a thirty-page season.
